chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluwayh (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: My uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim narrated to me. He said: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi narrated to me from his father Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Khalaf ibn Hammad al-Asadi, from Abu al-Hasan al-Abdi, from al-A'mash, from Abaya ibn Rib'i.

He said: A young man from the Ansar used to visit Abdullah ibn Abbas, and Abdullah would honour him and bring him close. It was said to him: You honour this young man and bring him close, yet he is a wicked young man who goes to the graves and exhumes them at night! So Abdullah ibn Abbas said: If that is the case, inform me.

He said: The young man went out one night wandering through the graves, and Abdullah ibn Abbas was informed of that. He went out to see what would come of his affair, and stood at a distance watching him from where the young man could not see him. He said: He entered a grave that had been dug, then lay down in the burial niche, and called out at the top of his voice:

'Woe is me! When I enter my burial niche alone, and the earth beneath me speaks, saying: No welcome and no greeting to you! I hated you while you were on my back, so how about now that you are in my belly! Rather, woe is me when I look at the prophets standing, and the angels in rows — who tomorrow will save me from Your justice? Who among the wronged will deliver me? Who will protect me from the punishment of the Fire? I disobeyed one who is not to be disobeyed. I made promises to my Lord time after time, yet He found no sincerity nor loyalty in me.'

He kept repeating these words and weeping. When he came out of the grave, Ibn Abbas embraced him and hugged him, then said to him: 'The best of grave-openers! The best of grave-openers! Your grave-opening is not for sins and transgressions.' Then they parted.

key_terms.اللَّحْد: The lahd — the niche carved into the side of a grave where the body is placed in Islamic burial
key_terms.عَدْل: Justice/divine reckoning — here refers to God's just judgment on the Day of Resurrection
key_terms.نَبَّاش: Grave-opener/exhumer — one who digs up graves; here used ironically in praise
key_terms.وَفَاء: Loyalty/fulfillment of promises — keeping one's covenant with God
key_terms.وَيْح: Woe/alas — an expression of lamentation or grief

ai.seo_question: What is the story of the young Ansari man who lay in a grave and was praised by Ibn Abbas?
ai.summary: This narrative from Al-Amali of Shaykh Saduq recounts how Ibn Abbas, the great companion and Quranic exegete, discovers that a young Ansari man he held in high esteem was secretly going to graveyards at night — not to desecrate graves, but to lie in an open grave and contemplate his own death and accountability before God. The story illustrates the profound spiritual practice of muraqabah (self-watchfulness) and tafakkur fi al-mawt (meditation on death) that was practiced by pious Muslims, and Ibn Abbas's wisdom in praising rather than condemning the young man once the truth was revealed. The expression 'the best of grave-openers' (niam al-nabbash) is a powerful rhetorical reversal — the one who seemed to be committing a grave sin was in fact engaging in the deepest spiritual introspection.
